This normalization can create a cycle where individuals see their peers using drugs as a means of stress relief, leading them to believe it's a socially acceptable solution.

It's important to recognize that drug use can have serious consequences, both for individuals and society as a whole. Addiction, health problems, and criminal activity are just a few of the potential negative outcomes associated with drug use. By normalizing drug use, we risk downplaying these risks and failing to address the underlying issues that lead to drug abuse.

In conclusion, the normalization of drug use in our society is a complex issue with multiple contributing factors. original_text:
# Body

RAM doesn't generate nearly as much heat as CPUs or GPUs, so it's often overlooked. Here's what you should know:

**Heat Limits:**
- Most modern DDR4 and DDR5 RAM is rated to handle temperatures up to 85-95°C before performance degrades or damage occurs
- However, you'll rarely see RAM get that hot in a properly ventilated case

**Typical Gaming Temps:**
- **Normal range:** 40-55°C during gaming
- **Warm but fine:** 55-65°C
- **Getting hot:** 65-75°C (time to check your case airflow)
- **Concerning:** 75°C+ (definitely improve cooling)

**Factors that affect RAM temperature:**
- Case airflow is the biggest factor
- CPU cooler placement (can block air from reaching RAM)
- Ambient room temperature
- Overclocking (will increase temps significantly)
- RAM location on the motherboard

**Real talk:** Unless you're severely overclocking or have terrible case airflow, you probably won't have RAM heat issues. Most air-cooled PCs keep RAM comfortably cool. If you're worried, make sure your case has decent intake and exhaust fans.

If you're consistently hitting 70°C+ on RAM during gaming, I'd focus on improving overall case airflow before worrying about RAM-specific cooling solutions.

Most manufacturers rate their modules for operation up to 95°C, but pushing past 85°C for extended periods can lead to system crashes, memory errors, or hardware degradation over time.

*   **Idle:** 30°C–40°C
*   **Under Gaming Load:** 45°C–60°C

If you are running high-voltage sticks (like overclocked DDR5 with tight timings) or if your RAM is positioned in a "dead zone" for airflow (like directly behind a massive CPU air cooler or a hot GPU), you might see them creep into the 65°C–70°C range. 

**How to check yours:**
You can use software like **HWiNFO64** to monitor your "DIMM Temperatures." 

**When to worry:**
If you find your RAM is consistently exceeding 75°C while gaming, you might want to look into improving your case airflow (adjusting fan curves) or ensuring your RAM isn't being heat-soaked by your GPU. It’s been eight months. The first few weeks were all dramatic—clear mornings, restless nights, the novelty of remembering every conversation. After that, the surprises started to fade, and I expected the rest of life to reorganize itself around the single fact that I wasn’t drinking anymore.  

It hasn’t. My inbox is still a mess. The same three friends still cancel plans. My cat still throws up on the rug at 3 a.m. On weekends the group chat fills with photos from bars I used to close, and I react with the same thumbs-up I always have; nobody notices the difference.  

What’s changed is microscopic. I fall asleep with the light off instead of waking to it. My hands don’t shake while I tie my shoes. The margin between “tired” and “hungover” is suddenly visible. But the big scenery—job, city, people, weather—looks exactly the way it did.  

I thought sobriety would feel like walking through a different landscape. It feels more like someone quietly swapped the soundtrack. Same room, same furniture, same window, just quieter.

prompt: Write just the body of a Reddit post titled "This for all the dead homies". Do not repeat the title.
original_text:
*lights a candle and pours one out*  

Y’all know the drill. Every time the block gets quiet, I hear their names echo off the bricks. They ain’t here for the new sneakers, the new phones, the new beef. They’re frozen in time—same faded hoodies, same lopsided smiles in pictures we still double-tap like they’ll text back.  

We said we’d make it out together. College apps on the same kitchen table, job interviews in the same busted button-ups, studio sessions with the same blown speakers. Now the only thing we share is a group chat that lights up on birthdays nobody answers.  

I still hit the corner store at 2 a.m. out of habit, still order their usual sandwich like muscle memory might resurrect them. The cashier still rings it up twice—force of habit. We both pretend not to notice.  

To the ones who never saw 21, the ones whose mamas still set an extra plate, the ones whose little brothers wear their chains like armor: we carry you in every W. Every time the rent’s paid on time, every time a case gets dismissed, every time the needle doesn’t touch skin—that’s your win too.  

Miss y’all loud. Miss y’all quiet. Miss y’all in the intro of every track I can’t finish.  

Stay dangerous and stay alive—for them.

I've been living in my car for about three months now. Started after I couldn't keep up with rent and my roommate situation fell apart. I work a full-time job but between car repairs and other bills, I just couldn't make the numbers work anymore.

I sleep in a Walmart parking lot most nights since it's well-lit and they don't seem to mind. I have a gym membership for showers and use a small camping stove to cook simple meals when I can. Most of my stuff is in storage, but I've got the essentials in the car - clothes, laptop for work, and a few comfort items.

The hardest parts are the lack of privacy and the constant low-level stress. Finding places to park overnight without getting hassled, dealing with the weather, and just the mental toll of not having a real home. I've got a decent savings goal I'm working toward, but it feels like two steps forward, one step back sometimes.

Just wanted to put this out there since I don't really talk about it with people in my day-to-day life.
